extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy (general educated public; scholars of metaphysics)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length philosophical treatment of death and the indestructibility of our true nature, arguing from empirical observation, metaphysical distinctions (will vs knowledge), and naturalistic considerations. Presents claims about why death need not be regarded as an absolute evil and offers lines of argument for the persistence of the 'true' principle of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear of death derives from the blind will to live
rubrics_metrics.description: The fear of death is a priori the reverse side of the will to live; it proceeds entirely and alone from the blind will, not from knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge is adventitious and works against the will: when knowledge conquers, the man faces death courageously and composedly, which is hailed as the triumph of knowledge over the blind will. Examples: brutes share fear of death despite ignorance; the will's attachment to life is irrational from a knowing standpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: From the standpoint of knowledge, death is no evil (Epicurean claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consciousness ceases with life, and absence of consciousness is not an evil; 'Death does not concern us' because when we are death is not, and when death is we are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: every good or evil presupposes existence and consciousness; therefore non-existence cannot be an evil. Analogies: sleep and swoon (loss of consciousness) are known and trusted as containing no evil; citations: Epicurus, Socrates, Voltaire.

rubrics_metrics.name: The annihilation of the organism is not equivalent to annihilation of the underlying life-principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Consciousness has always shown itself as product and result of organised life, arising and sinking with bodily conditions; the cessation of organised life (the body) does not justify concluding the annihilation of the unknown force that actuated it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations: consciousness varies with health, sleep, madness; derangement can even heighten other forces. Analogies: stopping of a pendulum doesn't annihilate gravitation; death may show disappearance of a manifestation but not the underlying force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperishability of true nature indicated by permanence of matter and natural forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Matter and natural forces (including the vital force seen as a natural force) remain untouched by changing forms and states; their permanence affords evidence for the indestructibility of our true nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: the dust/ashes of a body will re-form into crystals, metals, plants, animals; matter's continuance can be viewed as a reflecion/image of the will. Caveat: this is an outline or simile, not the kind of proof consolations typically expect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical observation: death (the vanishing of consciousness) is often painless and akin to sleep or swoon
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjective moment of death concerns the vanishing of consciousness because brain activity ceases; this transition can be like sleep or swoon and is not necessarily painful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: accounts of fainting, drowning, carbon monoxide, hanging; violent wounds often not felt until after consciousness is gone; death from old age is a gradual fading with diminishing passions and impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death can be a relief or a welcome friend in cases of insuperable suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: For those with insuperable obstacles, incurable diseases, or inconsolable grief, death may be desired as a return into nature's 'womb'—a cession of goods of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: Hindus' two-faced Yama (fearful and benevolent). Emphasises that entry into death is often preceded by physical and moral conflict and is not a trivial escape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature treats individual life and death as indifferent; significance lies only in the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature exposes individuals to trivial accidents and blind chance, showing that the death or life of the individual is of no real significance to nature as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: insects crushed by a foot, fish in nets, predators; conclusion: if nature sends forth its children without protection, their fall is 'a mere jest' because they return to the mother's womb (the whole). Implication: adopting a higher viewpoint makes life and death indifferent as nature is indifferent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mourning for the post-mortem non-existence is irrationally asymmetric to pre-birth non-existence
rubrics_metrics.description: If non-existence after death were an evil, we would have to regard the time before our birth equally as an evil; but we do not, so mourning the eternity after death is illogical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: an infinite time has run before birth without trouble; by symmetry the eternity after death should not be more fearful. Kant’s ideality of time is noted as an alternative solution but not pursued here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent coming-into-being and passing-away of individuals is a superficial phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: The constant arising and passing away of organised beings cannot touch the root of things; it is a relative or phenomenal occurrence conditioned by our intellect, masking a persistent underlying nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim: the universal or Idea in particulars points toward this conviction; small minds that only know particulars fear annihilation, while higher capacity minds see the universal in the particular and thereby ease terrors about death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of materialism and idealism at their correct level: each point of view truthfully reflects aspects of indestructibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Crude materialism represents indestructibility through permanence of matter; absolute idealism (and naturalism of forces) represents it through ubiquity and eternity of natural forces—each is true from its definite point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: philosophical systems are one-sided but not absolutely false; the highest standpoint surveys them all and shows their relative truth and falseness. Use this to support the claim that living beings do not suffer absolute annihilation through death.
